items.summary: Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants. Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks. We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.
items.title: Beyond LLM Wrappers: Context Engineering and the Three-Engine Architecture for Reliable Financial AI

items.summary: Description This repository provides supporting data products, analysis code, and reproducibility materials for an independent evaluation of the original satellite-derived modified temperature–humidity index (MTHI) proposed by Feng et al. (2020), using ground-observed air-based temperature–humidity index (THI) as the reference quantity. The study examines two distinct measurement tasks: (1) numerical estimation of air-based THI under frozen cross-network calibration, and (2) within-date spatial ranking of observed air-based THI across urban monitoring stations. The development dataset comprises 849 matched station-date observations from 109 stations across 18 dates in Leuven, Belgium (2021–2022). The independent external evaluation uses 249 matched observations from 19 urban stations across 20 dates in Novi Sad, Serbia (2016–2017). The predefined spatial-ranking analysis includes 197 observations across 13 qualifying dates. The numerical evaluation considers four predictor configurations: LST alone, the original Feng MTHI, LST and NDMI, and LST, NDMI and land surface emissivity. Model selection and calibration were performed using the Leuven development data, with the resulting configurations frozen before external evaluation. The repository supports verification of the reported numerical comparisons, spatial-ranking analyses, uncertainty assessments, and associated sensitivity analyses. The accompanying README documents the included files, their provenance, processing procedures, and reproducibility instructions. Any restrictions on redistribution of third-party observational or satellite data are documented separately. This archive does not constitute a validation of physiological heat stress, thermal perception, or human heat-health risk.
items.title: Reproducibility Data and Code for Evaluating Satellite-Derived MTHI Against Urban Air-Based THI

items.summary: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
items.title: Agentic process evidence

items.summary: This version (v1.4) extends the reproducibility package for “Before the weights: a validated admission gate for data-derived decision inputs, demonstrated on aggregate inward FDI” (Results in Engineering, manuscript RINENG-D-26-21905). It adds the records of a prospective, prespecified, synthetic-only benchmark comparing the frozen admission gate (G) with two simpler calibrated admission rules: a Ridge-only rule (A) and a single-split rule (B). The principal finding is unfavourable to the gate. At the smaller planted effect (δ = 0.005), G admitted 27 of 50 cases, A admitted 26 of 50, and B admitted 49 of 50. None of the three rules admitted any of 50 synthetic null or 40 persistence-matched null candidates at their calibrated operating points. The prespecified outcome labels were “No statistically resolved difference” for A and “Evidence favouring the comparator” for B. The comparison is conditional on the tested synthetic designs. It does not establish equal population-level false-admission rates, demonstrate downstream decision improvements, or test genuinely environment-dependent planted effects. The deposit contains the benchmark protocol, implementation, calibration records, seed registry, 190-cell execution return, reduction report, execution history, and independent verification records. Certain operational records have been anonymised to protect identifying information. The included anonymisation map links the public files to their original hash-bound verification records. The public reproduction procedure independently reproduces the scientific reduction, with its documented protocol-hash substitution. The previously published v1.3 record remains unchanged. Consult README.md inside the archive for the reproduction instructions, scientific limitations, and relationship between the public derivative and the verified originals.
items.title: Before the Weights: Reproducibility package for a validated admission gate for data-derived inputs to mineral-resource decision support

items.summary: A research field records its open problems in surveys, keynotes and community reports. Those are prose, written every few years, and nobody can ask them who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. We argue the problems should be data, and we build the system that makes them so: a hand-curated problem layer carried in unchanged, under an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database and queryable from one language. A language model does four jobs -- per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdict, and idea generation -- each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. We report a study on two curated catalogs, database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), each with a prior catalog-only graph. The rebuilt graph answers every question the catalog-only graph answered -- 47 of 47 on databases, 34 of 35 on AI -- plus questions the catalog-only graph refused: recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers bearing on a problem (336 problems, 770 works on databases). The capability we most wanted does not survive its own audit. Of 41 solves and refutes verdicts hand-checked against the papers, 9 are correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong; no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproves an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closes the central question. We report that failure in full and draw the design conclusion: a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied, making the human reviewer part of the architecture. We close with the data-engineering problems this raises: entity resolution across curated and harvested layers, verifying model status claims, freshness under source quotas, and evaluation without ground truth.
items.title: Rebuilding a Field's Open-Problem Catalog from the Literature: A Two-Layer Knowledge Graph, and Why Status Must Stay Proposed

items.summary: TRUSTWORTHY MANUFACTURING AND DIGITAL QUALITY PASSPORTS FOR BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT Manufacturing Evidence x Digital Traceability x Quality Release This 770-page Research Working Edition develops a falsification-oriented, nonclinical architecture for proving whether every biomedical micro/nanorobot product or batch can be linked to sufficient material, tool, model, process, test and failure evidence for an independent team to reconstruct its release rationale. It distinguishes record completeness from product qualification and treats physical identity, typed provenance, signature status, version compatibility, raw functional evidence, uncertainty, recall and retirement as separate scientific objects. The monograph contains 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 single-page investigations, 200 differentiated Research Gates and 33 genuinely distinguishable Phoenix Answer Embryos. The minimum demonstrator conceals three critical evidence gaps inside a signed passport and tests whether an independent audit refuses release without original-author assistance. A critical missing ancestor, ambiguous product identity, unverifiable signature, incompatible model evidence or unreplayable release decision is a hard veto. This is a prospective scientific architecture, not an executed clinical or regulatory study. It does not claim in-body safety, therapeutic efficacy, regulatory approval or clinical benefit. DOI-linked publications support component methods and boundaries; they do not validate the integrated F25 system. Technical profile: 770 pages; approximately 166,832 English words; 30 formula families; 82 chapters; 410 single-page studies; 200 Research Gates; 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos; 22 DOI records; navigable bookmarks; sixfold QA. items.summary: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.
items.title: Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks

items.summary: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.
items.title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement

items.summary: Code S1 for The Algae Senate: a knowledge-graph-augmented AI co-scientist . This archive contains project-authored pipeline and analysis code only. It excludes publisher-licensed documents, manuscript files, data, run outputs, credentials, third-party code, and all OASIS/MiroFish material. The matching Git repository is https://github.com/olympus-terminal/algae-senate-code.
items.title: Algae Senate — Code S1: Pipeline and analysis code

items.summary: First CRAN release. Install with install.packages("glyospalettes") . 208 palettes from Onell Design's Glyos line and 18 Glyos-compatible partner lines, with ggplot2 scales, palette search by plotting use case, colour picking and combining, and designer credit lines for figure captions. Browse every palette at https://bmaitner.github.io/glyospalettes/articles/browse.html. What's new in 0.3.0 Fifteen new palettes from releases since the first sampling pass: the Paleolords Wave 1 figures (Dan Suarez's new Glyos-compatible line, listed under his company "Swamp City Collectibles" with the paleo_ prefix), plus new Battle Tribes, Mighty Maniax, Warlords of Wor, A/V Robot and Cappy Space figures. 208 palettes in total. New glyos_credit() writes a figure-caption or acknowledgments sentence naming the colorways used and the companies that designed them, and follows picks and combines back to their source palettes. citation("glyospalettes") now returns a reference for the package itself. New glyos_pick() pools the colors of one or more palettes (or of a whole company or product line), drops those with poor WCAG contrast against a light, dark or grayscale background, and returns the n colors whose closest pair is farthest apart in CIE Lab, optionally judged under simulated color-vision deficiency. New glyos_combine() takes one color from each of a set of palettes, so a product line becomes a categorical palette with one color per figure; distinct = TRUE spreads the choices out for legibility. Both return named vectors (color by source palette) and print with their provenance; picks draw their swatches on the background they were chosen for. These mirror tf_pick() and tf_team_palette() in the sibling transformerpalettes package.
items.title: bmaitner/glyospalettes: glyospalettes 0.3.0

items.summary: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have often originated in how their training data were generated. Whether the programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance is unknown. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the publicly advertised curricula of health AI education programs at U.S. universities, identified through a structured multisource web search between April and July 2026. Two investigators coded coverage of data provenance (structural, dataset limitations, or data management only), ethics, and sustainability; collaborative structure; technical prerequisites; and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors. The primary outcome was provenance coverage at the structural or dataset-limitations level. Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included. Ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%; 95% CI, 11.7 to 38.1), and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%; 95% CI, 7.9 to 31.9). None of the seven master's degree programs met the primary outcome, and no program addressed sustainability. Eighteen programs included team-based work, but only 5 assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds. Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; among the 51 whose gender could be determined, 66.7% were men. U.S. health AI education programs widely taught ethics but rarely taught how clinical data are produced. None addressed the environmental cost of computation, and most instructors came from computational disciplines.
items.title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs

items.summary: We consider three-dimensional imaging of compactly supported anisotropic electric media from fixed-frequency polarimetric Maxwell far-field data. Maxwell transversality creates an obstruction absent from scalar Born inversion: each measurement determines only a projected action of the tensor-valued Fourier transform. We first resolve this obstruction by a finite-dimensional polarimetric inversion. For a general complex $3\times3$ contrast, three incidence--observation configurations are necessary, and we give an explicit three-configuration design that is sufficient at every nonzero interior Fourier point. Its Gram determinant yields quantitative conditioning information and exhibits the loss of recoverability at the boundary of the accessible Fourier ball. After tensor demixing, the inverse problem reduces componentwise to restricted Fourier inversion on the unit ball, which we regularize by spectral cutoff in three-dimensional ball generalized prolate spheroidal wave functions. For discrete acquisition, a combined reconstruction error estimate separates the effects of measurement noise, polarimetric amplification, off-grid Fourier mismatch, quadrature error, Born modeling error, and spectral truncation. Numerical tests examine polarimetric conditioning and use analytically generated Born data to compare three- and six-configuration recovery and assess off-grid sensitivity. Reconstructions from full-Maxwell volume-integral data assess the effects of noise, wavenumber, and basis choice, as well as the recovery of different tensor components.
items.title: Polarimetric Low-Rank Imaging of Anisotropic Maxwell Media

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
items.title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Multi-agent search and coverage is critical to autonomous exploration, search-and-rescue, and defense applications. This paper investigates settings where a mobile sensor network is tasked with coordinating to discover the position of a stationary target within a bounded region. We develop a Bayesian update scheme where agents iteratively combine local uncertainties derived from their sensor measurements through inverse variance weighting to get a better global understanding of where the target may be located given some prior belief. Network agents' trajectories are governed by a primal-dual gradient update rule that simultaneously minimizes the expected sensing uncertainty and enforces network connectivity among the agents. We prove that the belief converges to the target under mild, planner-agnostic conditions, with an explicit exponential rate of false-hypothesis rejection and a bound on expected search time. Simulation results show that we can successfully find the target and collapse belief to the ground truth target location while ensuring connectivity of our sensor network. They also empirically confirm our theoretical bounds and revisiting assumption. Finally, we compare against a lawnmower sweep, showing that our method locates the target more quickly when the prior is informative.
items.title: Belief-Driven Search in Connectivity-Constrained Mobile Sensor Networks with Convergence Guarantees

items.summary: Recommender systems face a tension between broadening exposure to diverse viewpoints and avoiding interactions that reinforce extreme positions. This tension is especially consequential in already polarized populations. Here we investigate whether recommendation strategies can reverse polarization rather than merely slow its development. Building on the Attraction--Repulsion Model of opinion dynamics, we introduce two complementary design principles: Tolerance-aware recommendation, which seeks to learn each individual's tolerance for disagreement and reduces exposure to viewpoints beyond that tolerance, and adaptive diversification, which broadens exposure for agents with more extreme opinions while retaining stronger personalization for moderates. Agent-based experiments show that highly personalized recommendations intensify polarization under polarized initial conditions. Tolerance awareness alone primarily slows polarization, whereas combining it with adaptive diversification can reduce polarization below its initial level and, under suitable conditions, restore consensus. Additional experiments incorporating persistent extreme influencers and a spiral-of-silence mechanism show that the combined strategy can mitigate polarization under social pressure and selective participation. To examine whether these findings extend beyond predefined opinion-update rules, we repeat the experiments on a simulated social platform populated by 100 LLM-driven agents prompted to move toward opinions similar to their own and away from those that differ substantially. Across three runs, the combined strategy is again the only recommendation policy tested that reverses polarization in every run. These findings distinguish polarization prevention from reversal and identify tolerance-aware, adaptive exposure as a promising recommendation design principle for reconnecting divided populations.
items.title: Reversing Polarization through Tolerance-Aware Recommendation and Adaptive Diversification

items.summary: The allocation of electric vehicles to public charging stations is increasingly constrained by the fact that several heterogeneous facilities often serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information. An accept/reject decision that is defensible for one station may nevertheless reduce the efficiency of the charging district as a whole. We formulate this operational problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and examine whether Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), instantiated through QMIX, improves assignment performance relative to a cooperative Independent Q-Learning baseline (IQL). The evaluation uses a six-station urban network simulated with SUMO, five independent random seeds, 200 training episodes, and four traffic flux scenarios ranging from 100 to 250 vehicles/hour. Under this protocol, QMIX reaches a mean reward per evaluated decision of +0.776, versus +0.578 for IQL (delta = +0.198, seed-paired Cohens dz = 2.98, exact two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum attainable value at this sample size), and raises the acceptance rate from 72.4% to 94.0% (delta = +21.6 pp, dz = 5.24, Wilcoxon p = 0.0625). A five-variant ablation suggests this gain is primarily attributable to the CTDE architecture when holding cooperative reward terms fixed, though not formally isolated with a single seed. By contrast, cooperative reward shaping and experience sharing show no clear descriptive benefit and may slightly reduce performance. These findings support the view that, for multi-station charging assignment, coordination should be embedded in the learning architecture rather than added only through heuristic cooperation terms.
items.title: Cooperative EV Charging Assignment Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: A Comparison of QMIX and Independent Q-Learning Under Urban Traffic Uncertainty

items.summary: Electric vehicle (EV) charging stations integrating photovoltaic (PV) generation, battery storage, and bidirectional grid exchange must coordinate access to limited chargers with energy supply while considering both energy cost and carbon emissions. This paper proposes a solver-free greedy heuristic (SFGH) for dynamic vehicle scheduling (VS) and a twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) controller for carbon-aware energy dispatch (ED). SFGH assigns EVs according to reductions in service delays, and TD3 controls battery operation to balance energy costs and carbon emissions while meeting the resulting charging demand. The model allows both PV and battery exports, accounting for export revenue and carbon credits. Simulations on year-long case studies show that SFGH--TD3 achieves the lowest accumulated service delay, energy cost, and carbon emissions among the evaluated heuristic and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) configurations.
items.title: Electric Vehicle Scheduling and Carbon-Aware Energy Dispatch for Charging Stations

items.summary: We present posterior-landscape, a Python framework to identify and characterize morphological features in two-dimensional probability densities. The framework combines concepts from topological data analysis, statistical density-ridge estimation, and scale-space image analysis. It extracts localized concentrations, valleys, ridges, and changes of slope; for Bayesian reconstructions, it propagates uncertainty in feature recovery, geometry, and correspondence across posteriors. The framework also connects two-dimensional structures to features in one-dimensional marginals, and quantifies their correlation with other inferred parameters. We validate the method on controlled densities, and demonstrate its use on gravitational-wave population reconstructions, where it provides a systematic way to identify and interpret population features and assess which ones carry information relevant for cosmology. The resulting catalogues also offer a common morphological representation for future comparisons between predictions and population reconstructions.
items.title: posterior-landscape: morphological feature finding in two-dimensional probability densities

items.summary: Gravitational observations can leave material properties undetermined in two different ways: distinct states can have the same total source, and distinct spacetime histories can have the same retained observations. We organize these inverse problems in general relativity through a property-level identifiability criterion, with applications to stars and black hole candidates. Two ideal massless gases illustrate equal-source ambiguity: their temperatures differ by a factor of $(8/29)^{1/4}$ and their entropies differ while their stress-energy tensors agree. A separate causal-fluid example starts with identical sources and geometric data but different constitutive responses; the two models' curvature histories separate at linear order in proper time and their scale factors at cubic order. For black hole candidates, the relevant distinction is between stationary exterior parameters, perturbing fluxes and constituent history. The framework provides a test for whether retained data identify a material property, separating instantaneous source equality, history-wide source equality and observational projection.
items.title: Curvature Blindness: Material Inference in Stars and Black Hole Candidates

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.
items.title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
items.title: Agentic process evidence

items.summary: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have often originated in how their training data were generated. Whether the programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance is unknown. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the publicly advertised curricula of health AI education programs at U.S. universities, identified through a structured multisource web search between April and July 2026. Two investigators coded coverage of data provenance (structural, dataset limitations, or data management only), ethics, and sustainability; collaborative structure; technical prerequisites; and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors. The primary outcome was provenance coverage at the structural or dataset-limitations level. Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included. Ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%; 95% CI, 11.7 to 38.1), and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%; 95% CI, 7.9 to 31.9). None of the seven master's degree programs met the primary outcome, and no program addressed sustainability. Eighteen programs included team-based work, but only 5 assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds. Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; among the 51 whose gender could be determined, 66.7% were men. U.S. health AI education programs widely taught ethics but rarely taught how clinical data are produced. None addressed the environmental cost of computation, and most instructors came from computational disciplines.
items.title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs

items.summary: Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants. Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks. We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.
items.title: Beyond LLM Wrappers: Context Engineering and the Three-Engine Architecture for Reliable Financial AI

items.summary: Description This repository provides supporting data products, analysis code, and reproducibility materials for an independent evaluation of the original satellite-derived modified temperature–humidity index (MTHI) proposed by Feng et al. (2020), using ground-observed air-based temperature–humidity index (THI) as the reference quantity. The study examines two distinct measurement tasks: (1) numerical estimation of air-based THI under frozen cross-network calibration, and (2) within-date spatial ranking of observed air-based THI across urban monitoring stations. The development dataset comprises 849 matched station-date observations from 109 stations across 18 dates in Leuven, Belgium (2021–2022). The independent external evaluation uses 249 matched observations from 19 urban stations across 20 dates in Novi Sad, Serbia (2016–2017). The predefined spatial-ranking analysis includes 197 observations across 13 qualifying dates. The numerical evaluation considers four predictor configurations: LST alone, the original Feng MTHI, LST and NDMI, and LST, NDMI and land surface emissivity. Model selection and calibration were performed using the Leuven development data, with the resulting configurations frozen before external evaluation. The repository supports verification of the reported numerical comparisons, spatial-ranking analyses, uncertainty assessments, and associated sensitivity analyses. The accompanying README documents the included files, their provenance, processing procedures, and reproducibility instructions. Any restrictions on redistribution of third-party observational or satellite data are documented separately. This archive does not constitute a validation of physiological heat stress, thermal perception, or human heat-health risk.
items.title: Reproducibility Data and Code for Evaluating Satellite-Derived MTHI Against Urban Air-Based THI

items.summary: TRUSTWORTHY MANUFACTURING AND DIGITAL QUALITY PASSPORTS FOR BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT Manufacturing Evidence x Digital Traceability x Quality Release This 770-page Research Working Edition develops a falsification-oriented, nonclinical architecture for proving whether every biomedical micro/nanorobot product or batch can be linked to sufficient material, tool, model, process, test and failure evidence for an independent team to reconstruct its release rationale. It distinguishes record completeness from product qualification and treats physical identity, typed provenance, signature status, version compatibility, raw functional evidence, uncertainty, recall and retirement as separate scientific objects. items.summary: A research field records its open problems in surveys, keynotes and community reports. Those are prose, written every few years, and nobody can ask them who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. We argue the problems should be data, and we build the system that makes them so: a hand-curated problem layer carried in unchanged, under an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database and queryable from one language. A language model does four jobs -- per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdict, and idea generation -- each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. We report a study on two curated catalogs, database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), each with a prior catalog-only graph. The rebuilt graph answers every question the catalog-only graph answered -- 47 of 47 on databases, 34 of 35 on AI -- plus questions the catalog-only graph refused: recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers bearing on a problem (336 problems, 770 works on databases). The capability we most wanted does not survive its own audit. Of 41 solves and refutes verdicts hand-checked against the papers, 9 are correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong; no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproves an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closes the central question. We report that failure in full and draw the design conclusion: a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied, making the human reviewer part of the architecture. We close with the data-engineering problems this raises: entity resolution across curated and harvested layers, verifying model status claims, freshness under source quotas, and evaluation without ground truth.
items.title: Rebuilding a Field's Open-Problem Catalog from the Literature: A Two-Layer Knowledge Graph, and Why Status Must Stay Proposed

items.summary: PHOTOSTABILITY OF BOTANICAL ACTIVES AND PACKAGING ENGINEERING AT THE LIMIT 中文書名:植物活性成分光穩定性與包材工程極限 Photostability of Botanical Actives and Packaging Engineering at the Limit is a 777-page English research working monograph investigating three coupled but independently falsifiable questions: photochemical degradation of identifiable botanical marker compounds, wavelength-resolved optical transmission through real packaging, and the qualification of storage safety against oxygen ingress and unknown photoproducts. Its central claim is conditional, not asserted. A package that retains more apparent active compound after simulated light exposure may simply exclude oxygen, reduce lamp heating, alter extraction recovery, or hide degradation products. The proposed test therefore crosses films with matched oxygen-transmission rates but contrasting spectral transmittance, and films with matched optical protection but contrasting oxygen transport. Incident spectra, absorbed dose, headspace oxygen, intact parent, isomers and degradants must remain distinct physical measurements. The opening candidate relation D_light = integral over time and wavelength of E_lambda times A_lambda formalizes spectral exposure only within explicitly measured optical and unit conventions. Thirty mathematically diverse research plates specify physical construction, dimensions, assumptions, blind falsification and linked chapters. Eighty-two research chapters and 410 separate-page investigations explore botanical provenance, optical metrology, photochemistry, oxygen transport, package manufacture, chemical recovery, second-site requalification and governance of false-positive claims. Two hundred single-page Research Gates challenge identifiable observables and strong alternative explanations; thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos describe distinguishable scientific instruments, assay references, failure sentinels, and research inheritance objects. Each Gate preserves an adverse test and a successor handoff rather than presuming the hypothesis will win. Three author-designated STARLI mother works provide methodological ancestry in identity protection, functional requalification and uncertainty-aware sampling, not experimental evidence of this skincare application. External method references span IUPAC actinometry, ASTM optical transmission and oxygen permeation, curcumin and anthocyanin photochemistry, and barrier-film research. Their scientific domains and limits are explicitly differentiated. This manuscript is a prospective, nonclinical Research Working Edition, not a completed photostability campaign, human trial, proof of cosmetic efficacy, or regulatory approval. items.summary: This version (v1.4) extends the reproducibility package for “Before the weights: a validated admission gate for data-derived decision inputs, demonstrated on aggregate inward FDI” (Results in Engineering, manuscript RINENG-D-26-21905). It adds the records of a prospective, prespecified, synthetic-only benchmark comparing the frozen admission gate (G) with two simpler calibrated admission rules: a Ridge-only rule (A) and a single-split rule (B). The principal finding is unfavourable to the gate. At the smaller planted effect (δ = 0.005), G admitted 27 of 50 cases, A admitted 26 of 50, and B admitted 49 of 50. None of the three rules admitted any of 50 synthetic null or 40 persistence-matched null candidates at their calibrated operating points. The prespecified outcome labels were “No statistically resolved difference” for A and “Evidence favouring the comparator” for B. The comparison is conditional on the tested synthetic designs. It does not establish equal population-level false-admission rates, demonstrate downstream decision improvements, or test genuinely environment-dependent planted effects. The deposit contains the benchmark protocol, implementation, calibration records, seed registry, 190-cell execution return, reduction report, execution history, and independent verification records. Certain operational records have been anonymised to protect identifying information. The included anonymisation map links the public files to their original hash-bound verification records. The public reproduction procedure independently reproduces the scientific reduction, with its documented protocol-hash substitution. The previously published v1.3 record remains unchanged. Consult README.md inside the archive for the reproduction instructions, scientific limitations, and relationship between the public derivative and the verified originals.
items.title: Before the Weights: Reproducibility package for a validated admission gate for data-derived inputs to mineral-resource decision support

items.summary: The allocation of electric vehicles to public charging stations is increasingly constrained by the fact that several heterogeneous facilities often serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information. An accept/reject decision that is defensible for one station may nevertheless reduce the efficiency of the charging district as a whole. We formulate this operational problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and examine whether Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), instantiated through QMIX, improves assignment performance relative to a cooperative Independent Q-Learning baseline (IQL). The evaluation uses a six-station urban network simulated with SUMO, five independent random seeds, 200 training episodes, and four traffic flux scenarios ranging from 100 to 250 vehicles/hour. Under this protocol, QMIX reaches a mean reward per evaluated decision of +0.776, versus +0.578 for IQL (delta = +0.198, seed-paired Cohens dz = 2.98, exact two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum attainable value at this sample size), and raises the acceptance rate from 72.4% to 94.0% (delta = +21.6 pp, dz = 5.24, Wilcoxon p = 0.0625). A five-variant ablation suggests this gain is primarily attributable to the CTDE architecture when holding cooperative reward terms fixed, though not formally isolated with a single seed. By contrast, cooperative reward shaping and experience sharing show no clear descriptive benefit and may slightly reduce performance. These findings support the view that, for multi-station charging assignment, coordination should be embedded in the learning architecture rather than added only through heuristic cooperation terms.
items.title: Cooperative EV Charging Assignment Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: A Comparison of QMIX and Independent Q-Learning Under Urban Traffic Uncertainty

items.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on persistent memory and inter-agent communication. These capabilities create privacy risks that extend beyond individual interactions: a release appropriate in isolation may become inappropriate when combined with information previously disclosed to a recipient or propagated to downstream agents along the planned workflow. Existing Contextual Integrity (CI) mechanisms for agentic systems typically rely on local judgments that assess each disclosure in isolation, with or without regard to the recipient's history, but do not account for how information propagates downstream. However, compliance at the current boundary does not guarantee appropriateness across the workflow. We introduce Task-Graph Contextual Integrity (TG-CI), to our knowledge the first task-graph-native formalization of Contextual Integrity for multi-agent systems. TG-CI represents a workflow as a Multi-Agent Task Graph (MATG) and extends CI from atomic transfers to stateful, graph-level information flows by jointly considering an item's intended propagation scope and recipients' evolving disclosure states. We operationalize TG-CI through propagation-scoped authorization under two complementary policies: Full-Scope, which requires admissibility across the complete downstream scope, and Auto-Region, which confines each item to its maximal admissible region using lightweight frontier gates. We further introduce MAPLE-Bench, a benchmark of 144 cases across four scenarios that jointly vary MATG topology, disclosure history, compromised-agent placement, and item-level privacy policies. In our primary experimental configuration, TG-CI reduces the mean unauthorized disclosure count by 85.8-94.1% relative to the Local-History CI baseline, while retaining 93.6-96.1% of the baseline's task accuracy, with the two enforcement policies providing complementary privacy--cost--utility trade-offs.
items.title: Judging Before Propagation: Task-Graph Contextual Integrity for Multi-Agent Privacy

items.summary: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems
items.title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations

items.summary: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.

items.summary: Borrowed Youth: Demographic Change and Multinational Location Advantage explains how national cohort succession and international recruitment become firm-specific location advantages over a production commitment. Home-linked relationships, recruitment shared across foreign affiliates and admission institutions determine attainable replacement labour. Version 3.33.0 clarifies the empirical bridge and journal exposition. The model-to-data mapping distinguishes accessible worker stocks and annual arrival flows from their discounted service values. Table 3 now leads with the main engineering-life comparison, followed by the accounting and common-support benchmarks. The country equal-pricing contrasts are expressed as conditional investment changes holding total measured international services fixed, with full covariance and uncertainty preserved. These transformations introduce no additional test, observation or regression. The discussion relates demographic succession to resource bundling, human-capital access and multinational portfolios. The exact AI declaration, including all figures, is preserved. Previously reported scientific results are preserved. The article supplies an explicit economic bridge from project value to expected investment allocation under stated choice, capital-size, duration and disclosure conditions. It distinguishes capital expenditure from accumulated assets, whose interpretation additionally depends on investment histories, depreciation and valuation changes. The retained capital-expenditure analysis uses the existing demographic construction and controls. There are 82 matched records from ten firms and 36 after fixed-effect support. The nuisance design has rank 33; the five focal regressors have rank three. Independent projection confirms this failure. No duration coefficient, interval or p-value is identified; the result is not a zero effect. The public module reconstructs the aggregate rank and supplies licensed rerun code without redistributing issuer rows. The existing engineering-life asset comparison remains: 317 allocations from 32 manufacturers in nine hosts, contrast -110.25 (95 percent interval -520.28 to 299.78; positive-direction p=0.724). Joint positive pricing and rotation are unestablished (p=0.763), and the familywise contradiction test does not reject (p=0.712). Existing Holm-adjusted block probabilities are 0.113, 0.085 and 0.656. All original estimates, covariance matrices, equations, formal results and six figures are preserved. These conditional associations do not identify recruitment-caused host choices. The held Nitra-Puebla appraisal supplies a EUR106-226 million residual strategic hurdle and 2,834 planned direct jobs. At a five-percent reference rate this is EUR2,959-6,308 per planned job-year. The retained frontier states the additional net productive service needed to cover an assigned share, excluding previously priced labour effects and without fitting a recruitment share. Cost-saving bounds distinguish fixed-life value improvement from a unique switch across lives. No new sources or observations were acquired. The manuscript has 9,920 counted words, a 172-word abstract and 23 full substantive pages before references; the main PDF has 41 pages and the appendix 137. Regression tables retain three-decimal probabilities, no significance stars and economic magnitudes. Counts include abstract, text, references and transparency; separately placed exhibits and the online appendix are excluded. Start with README.txt. Current article, appendix and complete LaTeX are directly downloadable. Three current verified ZIP blocks and nine frozen complementary archives reconstruct the exact 1,908-file replication tree with 1,907 checksum entries. Licensed WRDS rows are excluded; subscriber queries and public aggregate reconstruction are supplied. Third-party rights remain. Literature PDFs are linked rather than redistributed. ChatGPT and Codex (OpenAI) were used in October 2026 for coding h

items.summary: Description This repository provides supporting data products, analysis code, and reproducibility materials for an independent evaluation of the original satellite-derived modified temperature–humidity index (MTHI) proposed by Feng et al. (2020), using ground-observed air-based temperature–humidity index (THI) as the reference quantity. The study examines two distinct measurement tasks: (1) numerical estimation of air-based THI under frozen cross-network calibration, and (2) within-date spatial ranking of observed air-based THI across urban monitoring stations. The development dataset comprises 849 matched station-date observations from 109 stations across 18 dates in Leuven, Belgium (2021–2022). The independent external evaluation uses 249 matched observations from 19 urban stations across 20 dates in Novi Sad, Serbia (2016–2017). The predefined spatial-ranking analysis includes 197 observations across 13 qualifying dates. The numerical evaluation considers four predictor configurations: LST alone, the original Feng MTHI, LST and NDMI, and LST, NDMI and land surface emissivity. Model selection and calibration were performed using the Leuven development data, with the resulting configurations frozen before external evaluation. The repository supports verification of the reported numerical comparisons, spatial-ranking analyses, uncertainty assessments, and associated sensitivity analyses. The accompanying README documents the included files, their provenance, processing procedures, and reproducibility instructions. Any restrictions on redistribution of third-party observational or satellite data are documented separately. This archive does not constitute a validation of physiological heat stress, thermal perception, or human heat-health risk.
items.title: Reproducibility Data and Code for Evaluating Satellite-Derived MTHI Against Urban Air-Based THI

items.summary: The allocation of electric vehicles to public charging stations is increasingly constrained by the fact that several heterogeneous facilities often serve the same stream of requests while observing only partial local information. An accept/reject decision that is defensible for one station may nevertheless reduce the efficiency of the charging district as a whole. We formulate this operational problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and examine whether Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE), instantiated through QMIX, improves assignment performance relative to a cooperative Independent Q-Learning baseline (IQL). The evaluation uses a six-station urban network simulated with SUMO, five independent random seeds, 200 training episodes, and four traffic flux scenarios ranging from 100 to 250 vehicles/hour. Under this protocol, QMIX reaches a mean reward per evaluated decision of +0.776, versus +0.578 for IQL (delta = +0.198, seed-paired Cohens dz = 2.98, exact two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0625, the minimum attainable value at this sample size), and raises the acceptance rate from 72.4% to 94.0% (delta = +21.6 pp, dz = 5.24, Wilcoxon p = 0.0625). A five-variant ablation suggests this gain is primarily attributable to the CTDE architecture when holding cooperative reward terms fixed, though not formally isolated with a single seed. By contrast, cooperative reward shaping and experience sharing show no clear descriptive benefit and may slightly reduce performance. These findings support the view that, for multi-station charging assignment, coordination should be embedded in the learning architecture rather than added only through heuristic cooperation terms.
items.title: Cooperative EV Charging Assignment Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: A Comparison of QMIX and Independent Q-Learning Under Urban Traffic Uncertainty

items.summary: This version (v1.4) extends the reproducibility package for “Before the weights: a validated admission gate for data-derived decision inputs, demonstrated on aggregate inward FDI” (Results in Engineering, manuscript RINENG-D-26-21905). It adds the records of a prospective, prespecified, synthetic-only benchmark comparing the frozen admission gate (G) with two simpler calibrated admission rules: a Ridge-only rule (A) and a single-split rule (B). The principal finding is unfavourable to the gate. At the smaller planted effect (δ = 0.005), G admitted 27 of 50 cases, A admitted 26 of 50, and B admitted 49 of 50. None of the three rules admitted any of 50 synthetic null or 40 persistence-matched null candidates at their calibrated operating points. The prespecified outcome labels were “No statistically resolved difference” for A and “Evidence favouring the comparator” for B. The comparison is conditional on the tested synthetic designs. It does not establish equal population-level false-admission rates, demonstrate downstream decision improvements, or test genuinely environment-dependent planted effects. The deposit contains the benchmark protocol, implementation, calibration records, seed registry, 190-cell execution return, reduction report, execution history, and independent verification records. Certain operational records have been anonymised to protect identifying information. The included anonymisation map links the public files to their original hash-bound verification records. The public reproduction procedure independently reproduces the scientific reduction, with its documented protocol-hash substitution. The previously published v1.3 record remains unchanged. Consult README.md inside the archive for the reproduction instructions, scientific limitations, and relationship between the public derivative and the verified originals.
items.title: Before the Weights: Reproducibility package for a validated admission gate for data-derived inputs to mineral-resource decision support

items.summary: Version 1.2 (28 October 2026) adds a notice on the arithmetic precision of the split‑Gibbs runs (NOTICE_v1.2.md), with the check behind it (TF32_CHECK.md, tf32_check_files.zip). DP1’s split‑Gibbs runs used reduced‑precision (TF32) matrix products, which a later like‑for‑like check found shift that sampler’s estimates, while its predictions ran in full float32. The split‑Gibbs null result therefore has a further candidate explanation that DP1 cannot separate. DPS is unaffected. No file of earlier versions has changed. A pre-specified pilot testing whether a blindness-risk score computed before any target data are seen ranks the realised blindness (undetected and uncovered error) of diffusion-prior inference on real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access. Study DP-A: weak attenuation (F = 32,000), 240 errors × 20 bases. Study DP-B: bounded-reach control, 120 errors × 20 bases. Two samplers: split-Gibbs plug-and-play (primary) and diffusion posterior sampling (secondary). It follows the learned (VAE) pilot, arXiv:2610.28155 (reproducibility package doi:10.5281/zenodo.23392686). The analysis plan, decision rules and fixed result sentences were approved by the author, and predictions and calibration were committed by SHA-256 hash, before any trial. The plan was not lodged with an external registry, so the study is described as pre-specified; the files named PREREG_… are that plan (their names, and the word "pre-registered" inside the hashed plan and the dated log, are kept unchanged so that the recorded hashes still match). Version 1.1 (26 October 2026) adds a post-hoc check of the linear response used by the blindness-risk score, specified in a dated plan and approved before any computation (response_check_plan_v1.md, response_check.py, response_check_results.json, RESPONSE_CHECK.md). Under the plan’s pre-specified reading, the response was not adequate for either sampler in either study, so the null result for the learned score does not separate the learned prior from this approximation. The pre-specified results of version 1.0 are unchanged. README.md and freeze_log.txt are updated accordingly.
items.title: BLINDSET diffusion-prior blind-set pilot: analysis plan, code, frozen predictions, trial records and results

items.summary: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
items.title: Agentic process evidence

items.summary: Raw surface EMG (13 shoulder and elbow muscles) and isometric force/torque recordings (6 channels), sampled at 1 kHz, from three chronic stroke survivors who performed a virtual reaching task in immersive virtual reality with their most affected arm. The virtual cursor was driven either by the measured isometric force (force control) or by the force estimated from EMG (myoelectric control). In myoelectric control, a patient-tailored assistive-adaptive algorithm projected the participant's muscle pattern towards a healthy reference pattern, with an assistance level progressively reduced across blocks. For each participant the dataset contains one session of 9 to 16 blocks (376 trials in total): a maximum voluntary contraction block, force-control baseline blocks and myoelectric-control blocks at different assistance levels. Each trial file contains the raw EMG, forces and torques, the force driving the cursor, the task state, the trial events and the trial metadata (target direction, block, assistance level). A configuration file per participant describes the channels, the sensor calibration and the block settings. The data are pseudonymised. The files are MATLAB v7 MAT-files that can be read in MATLAB and in Python (scipy.io.loadmat). See README.md for the full description of the files and variables. These data support: Nocilli M., d'Avella A., Berger D.J. (2025). A novel approach to promote upper-limb motor recovery in stroke survivors using assistive myoelectric control and adaptive visual feedback in virtual reality. Front. Bioeng. Biotechnol. 13:1628679. https://doi.org/10.3389/fbioe.2025.1628679  Funding: Italian Ministry of Health, European Union - NextGenerationEU - NRRP M6C2 - Investment 2.1, project PNRR-POC-2022-12375705, CUP J83C22002060007.
items.title: Raw EMG and isometric force data from a pilot study of assistive myoelectric control with adaptive visual feedback in virtual reality in chronic stroke survivors
